prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength brought optical time standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as a single two-person prize. After the first round I read the case as one idea and one realisation: choose the trapping wavelength so that the light shift cancels for the clock transition, and thousands of atoms can be held tightly, without Doppler or recoil shifts, and interrogated together. This idea was made to work, first by Katori and his collaborators and then at the accuracy frontier by Ye's group, and it has been reproduced with Sr, Yb and Hg in many laboratories, with agreeing frequency ratios and fibre-linked comparisons. The results that follow are physics, not only engineering: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants and on dark-matter couplings, and a clear route to redefining the second. Five of eight colleagues now prefer this configuration, but I do not lean on that count. I lean on the fact that the credit can be defended from the historical record and the result has stood for twenty years. I have also considered a two-part prize and decided against it. The only way to add a second achievement within three people would leave one laureate for a part such as IceCube or the Hubbard-model work, and that would damage a case that is clean as it stands.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that precision timekeeping has been honoured several times (Ramsey 1989, Hall and Hansch 2005, Wineland and Haroche 2012), so a sceptic can call lattice clocks a refinement and not a new phenomenon. Danielsson and Mehlig press this from different directions, and I cannot fully dismiss it. Second, the priority record is not settled by the committee files alone: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hollberg, Hinkley and others contributed, and a narrow two-name credit leaves them out. Third, the second has not yet been redefined, and one can say the full consequences are still to come. Finally, I am myself an atomic theorist who works on precision calculations, so I may overrate the elegance of the clock result relative to a measurement that opens a new window on the sky.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers IceCube (B010) with Halzen and Karle as a discovery in the plainest sense, and in his round-1 reply to me called B043 mature and well confirmed but a refinement of time-keeping in which no new phenomenon was found. He asked whether the redefinition of the second would precede our decision.
responses.response: I take the discovery point seriously, and it is where I am least certain of my own ground, since I defer to you and Pearce on neutrino astronomy. On the redefinition, I do not think it is a precondition: it is a consequence of the accuracy already demonstrated, and the evidence of a result is its reproduction in independent laboratories, not a decision by the metrology bodies. As for novelty, the lattice clock did produce something unexpected, namely that a many-atom neutral system can match and then exceed the best single ion, which few expected before the magic-wavelength idea. That is a statement about what a quantum system can do when its perturbations are understood. I agree that the diffuse neutrino flux is a real discovery, but your own doubts about the Halzen, Karle and Yoshida split, and the lack of a second telescope at similar sensitivity, make me keep B010 as an alternative and not as my preferred part this year.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers the theory of two-dimensional melting (B020) for its simple universal mechanism, and asks whether the committee is weighing mature precision metrology above a conceptual advance, and whether Ye's role is only implementation of Katori's idea.
responses.response: I agree that the Halperin-Nelson-Young mechanism is an elegant and clean three-person attribution, and I share your wish to honour theorists while they can be honoured. I do not think unanimity among experimentalists is an argument, and I have tried to weigh the science alone. Two points keep me from moving: you yourself note that the first-order versus continuous question is system dependent and that the 2016 prize may be seen as covering the defect idea, and no other colleague ranks it. On Ye, you are right that his role is more than implementation. His group made the accuracy step to 1e-18, studied the many-body and collisional physics of the clock, and built the systematic intercomparisons that convinced the community. I would therefore describe his credit as realisation at the frontier and keep the citation tied to lattice clocks, not to combs or molecules.

responses.point: Olsson supports B043 with a narrow citation, arguing that the magic-wavelength statement can be made without leaning on the earlier prizes, and asks whether the pair should be broadened because Takamoto and others realised the first lattice clock with Katori.
responses.response: I agree with your test that the achievement should be statable without reference to 2005 or 2012, and I have kept the citation in that form. On broadening, I would not add Takamoto: the Nobel rule limits us to three, and the 2006 and 2008 demonstrations were work in Katori's group, so his claim is already carried by Katori's name. Adding Lemonde or Ludlow would open a priority question that the files do not resolve. I support your suggestion that the early record be checked by an outside expert before the final vote, and if that review pointed to a different third person, I would want to hear which result in the primary literature supports it before I changed the configuration.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved clocks to the top, adopted a narrow citation without Ye's comb and molecule work, and asked which part of the lattice clock claim colleagues think is already covered by 2005 or 2012.
responses.response: My answer to your question is that none of the claim is covered. The comb gave a way to count optical cycles, and ion trapping gave single-particle control, but neither addresses how to interrogate a large number of neutral atoms without the trap perturbing the transition. That is what the magic wavelength does, and it changed the statistics and the systematics, which is why lattice clocks overtook ion clocks. I note your hesitation that a clock is a window and not a discovery from nature. I accept that this is a matter of taste on which reasonable members differ, and I leave it as such. I also agree with the approach of a single part, since pairing the clocks with another achievement would push past three names.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat lattice clocks as a distinct invention or as a continuation of the precision-timekeeping line honoured in 2005 and 2012.
The priority record among Katori, Ye, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Hollberg; I rely on an outside expert to confirm that two names are enough.
Whether to wait for the redefinition of the second; I think it is a confirming milestone and not a condition, but I cannot be sure my colleagues agree.
Comparative merit against IceCube (B010) and Hubbard-model simulation (B006), where I defer to colleagues on the astroparticle side and where Bloch, Cirac, Greiner and Zoller would need four names.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, and I know many people in the atomic, molecular and optical community. As far as my profile shows, none of the shortlisted candidates (Katori, Ye, Halzen, Karle, Yoshida, Bloch, Zoller and others) is a collaborator, coauthor or colleague of mine, so I see no need to recuse. The round-1 chair summary records no new conflict for me.
